core: How a food and beverage (F&B) operation is structured: front-of-house (FOH) vs back-of-house (BOH) and the main outlet types
Service styles: a la carte vs table d'hote menus; plate (American), family-style, platter (Russian), cart/gueridon (French), buffet, and banquet service
Food cost percentage = cost of food sold / food sales, and using a target food-cost percentage to set a menu price
Contribution margin (menu selling price minus item food cost) and its role in menu analysis
Menu engineering: classifying items by popularity and profitability into stars, plowhorses, puzzles, and dogs (Kasavana & Smith, 1982)
supporting: Food service manager occupational role and U.S. labor data (BLS)
Guest check average and table turnover as operating measures
The 70% menu-mix popularity rule used in the Kasavana-Smith model
outOfScope: Food safety: HACCP, holding temperatures, pathogens, sanitation procedures - owned by Food Safety
Event and banquet planning in depth (BEOs, room sets, event logistics) - owned by Event Planning
Revenue management, RevPAR, ADR, and occupancy pricing discipline - lodging topics
Hotel departmental structure and the rooms division - owned by Hotel Operations

claims.claim: A food and beverage operation divides into the front of house (FOH), the guest-facing areas where guests are welcomed, seated, and served, and the back of house (BOH), primarily the kitchen plus dishwashing, storage, and the back office.

Restaurants use several table-service styles, including plate service (the most common), family-style, platter service, cart/tableside service, and buffet service, which differ in where food is portioned and how much tableside labor and guest self-service are involved.

Food cost percentage equals the cost of food sold divided by food sales (expressed as a percent), and many full-service restaurants target roughly 28-35 percent, with about 30 percent a common benchmark.
The food-cost pricing method sets a menu price by dividing an item's food cost by the target food-cost percentage, so a $6.30 item at a 30% target prices to $21.00.
Contribution margin for a menu item is its selling price minus its food cost; keeping contribution margins high, not merely keeping food-cost percentage low, is central to menu profitability.

Menu engineering, introduced by Michael L. Kasavana and Donald I. Smith in their 1982 book 'Menu Engineering: A Practical Guide to Menu Analysis', classifies each menu item by two dimensions, popularity (sales volume) and profitability (contribution margin), into four categories: stars (high/high), plowhorses (high popularity/low margin), puzzles (low popularity/high margin), and dogs (low/low).

Food service managers coordinate the daily operations of restaurants and other establishments that prepare and serve food and beverages; the occupation had a median annual wage of $65,310 in May 2024, held about 352,800 jobs in 2024, and is projected to grow about 6 percent from 2024 to 2034 with roughly 42,000 openings per year.

Operators track additional measures such as guest check average (total sales divided by number of guests) and table turnover (guests served divided by number of tables) to judge how efficiently an outlet uses its seats.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Naming of service styles differs across texts and traditions.
positions: Some texts label plate service 'American service', platter service 'Russian service', and cart/gueridon service 'French service'
Open OER texts (e.g., the SUNY chapter) use the plainer plate/family/platter/cart/buffet labels
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson gives both the plain-English and classical names, and treats the classical labels as regionally variable conventions rather than fixed standards.

positions: Practice ranges roughly 25-40% depending on concept, menu mix, and market
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as a target band (about 28-35%, ~30% common) rather than a universal number, and used only to illustrate the pricing arithmetic.
